result.title: Building analogue instruments
result.blurb: Start with a simple oscillator and build up. These give you the theory and the build guides, and a pile of inspiration.

result.title: Building digital instruments
result.blurb: A microcontroller plus a few sensors goes a long way. Pick a platform and a software environment, and follow a project close to what you want to make.

result.title: Touch-based instruments
result.blurb: Turn fruit, paint, metal or anything conductive into a controller — often without writing a line of code.

result.title: Acoustic and physical instruments
result.blurb: Often the best resource is a room full of people with tools. Find a makerspace, then look at how others have built instruments from found materials.

result.title: Accessible instrument design
result.blurb: Designing with disabled musicians from the start leads to better instruments for everyone.

install.question: What will trigger or drive the sound?

result.title: Touch-triggered installations
result.blurb: Conductive materials and simple boards let visitors play the work with their hands.

result.title: Sensor-driven installations
result.blurb: Read the world with sensors, then map it to sound. Low-latency audio platforms and visual patching tools both work well here.

result.title: Generative and software-driven sound
result.blurb: Learn a sound programming environment, then let your rules make the music.

result.title: Finding your way in
result.blurb: Look at what other people have built, then pick a small first project and join a community.

options.label: Seeing what other sound artists do

result.title: Recording and sampling
result.blurb: Collect sounds, then learn to shape them.

result.title: Coding sound
result.blurb: Free environments with big communities and lots of tutorials.

result.title: Learning from other practitioners
result.blurb: Browse practitioners and past Hackoustic artists, then follow the links they share.
